los.text: Describe the causes, diagnosis, signs and symptoms, and principles for treatment and management of viral infections (measles, rubella, influenza, varicella, tetanus, covid-19; include vaccination principles)
los.html:
InfectionFeaturesDiagnosis / treatment
Measles (paramyxovirus, very contagious, airborne)
  • Prodrome: fever, 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots → maculopapular rash from behind ears spreading down.
  • Complications: pneumonia (commonest death), otitis media, encephalitis, SSPE (years later), immunosuppression
Saliva/oral fluid PCR or IgM; notify; supportive; vitamin A (children, LMICs); post-exposure MMR within 72 h or HNIG for vulnerable
Rubella (togavirus)Mild fever, pink rash, post-auricular/occipital lymphadenopathy, arthralgia. Congenital rubella (1st trimester): deafness, cataracts, PDA, microcephalyIgM/PCR; notifiable; check immunity pre-pregnancy
InfluenzaAbrupt fever, myalgia, cough, headachePCR; oseltamivir for at-risk
Varicella (VZV)Crops of itchy vesicles at different stages, centripetal; complications: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia (adults, smokers, pregnancy), encephalitis/cerebellitis; shingles laterClinical; aciclovir for adults, immunosuppressed, pregnant; VZIG for exposed susceptible pregnant/immunosuppressed
Tetanus (Clostridium tetani toxin, a bacterium)Contaminated wounds; trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, muscle spasms, opisthotonus, autonomic instabilityClinical; human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, ICU; booster/vaccine
COVID-19See week 116PCR/LFT
  • Vaccination principles: induce immunological memory without disease.
    • Live attenuated (MMR, varicella, LAIV, rotavirus, BCG, yellow fever: strong, long-lasting; avoid in immunosuppression/pregnancy)
    • inactivated (polio IPV, influenza injectable)
    • subunit/conjugate (Hib, pneumococcal, MenACWY: polysaccharide conjugated to protein → T-cell dependent response in infants)
    • toxoid (tetanus, diphtheria)
    • recombinant (HBV, HPV, Shingrix)
    • mRNA/viral vector (COVID-19).
    • Primary course → boosters
    • herd immunity threshold depends on R₀ (measles ~95%).

los.text: Explain the role of T and B lymphocytes in the specific and adaptive immune response (compare normal and abnormal function)
los.html:
Antigen presentation
  • Dendritic cells present peptide on MHC II to CD4⁺ T cells and on MHC I (cross-presentation) to CD8⁺.
  • Activation needs signal 1 (TCR–peptide–MHC), signal 2 (co-stimulation: CD28–B7) and cytokines (signal 3).
  • Without co-stimulation → anergy.
CD4⁺ helper subsets
  • Th1 (IFN-γ; activates macrophages vs intracellular pathogens)
  • Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; IgE, eosinophils, parasites, allergy)
  • Th17 (IL-17; neutrophils, extracellular bacteria/fungi, autoimmunity)
  • Tfh (help B cells in germinal centres)
  • Treg (FOXP3; IL-10/TGF-β; tolerance).
CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cellsRecognise peptide on MHC I (all nucleated cells) → kill virus-infected/tumour cells via perforin/granzymes and Fas–FasL.
B cells
  • BCR binds native antigen
  • → internalise and present on MHC II
  • → T-cell help (CD40L–CD40)
  • → class switching and affinity maturation (somatic hypermutation) in germinal centres
  • → plasma cells + memory B cells.
  • T-independent antigens (polysaccharides) → mainly IgM (poor in children <2, hence conjugate vaccines).
MemorySecondary response faster, larger, higher-affinity IgG.
Abnormal function
  • Immunodeficiency: primary (X-linked agammaglobulinaemia: no B cells; CVID; DiGeorge: no thymus → T-cell defect; SCID) or secondary (HIV destroys CD4 cells; chemotherapy, steroids, malnutrition).
  • Autoimmunity: loss of tolerance (T1DM, MS, RA).
  • Hypersensitivity (next LO).
  • Lymphoid malignancy (lymphoma, CLL, myeloma).

los.text: Describe the four types of hypersensitivity reactions (Types I-IV), their underlying immunological mechanisms and typical clinical features
los.html:
TypeMechanismTimingExamples
I – Immediate (anaphylactic)IgE on mast cells/basophils cross-linked by allergen → degranulation (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes)MinutesAnaphylaxis, allergic asthma, hay fever, urticaria, food/drug allergy
II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxicIgG/IgM against cell-surface or matrix antigens → complement, opsonisation, ADCC, or receptor stimulation/blockingHours–daysHaemolytic transfusion reaction, haemolytic disease of newborn, AIHA, ITP, Goodpasture's, Graves' (stimulating), myasthenia gravis (blocking), pemphigus, rheumatic fever
III – Immune complexSoluble antigen–antibody complexes deposit in vessels/tissues → complement activation → neutrophil inflammationHours–days (1–3 weeks for serum sickness)SLE, post-streptococcal GN, serum sickness, Arthus reaction, extrinsic allergic alveolitis (with IV), RA vasculitis
IV – Delayed (cell-mediated)T cells (CD4 Th1 → macrophages; CD8 cytotoxicity), no antibody48–72 hContact dermatitis (nickel), Mantoux test, TB granulomas, transplant rejection, T1DM, MS, SJS/TEN
  • Clinical features: I (urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension; ↑ mast cell tryptase)
    • II (cytopenias, organ-specific)
    • III (fever, rash, arthralgia, nephritis, ↓ complement)
    • IV (eczematous rash, induration).
  • Mnemonic ACID: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic, Immune complex, Delayed.

los.text: Describe how immune reactions are used in the laboratory for the diagnosis of infectious diseases
sessions: BMS 1: Immune reactions in the diagnosis of infection
los.html:
Serology (antibody detection)
  • IgM = recent/acute infection
  • IgG = past infection/immunity (or rising titre ×4 in paired sera 10–14 days apart = acute).
  • Avidity testing dates infection (low avidity = recent).
Antigen detection
  • Uses known antibodies to detect microbial antigen: ELISA
  • Lateral flow (COVID-19, malaria, urinary pneumococcal/Legionella, C. difficile GDH, H. pylori stool antigen)
  • Immunofluorescence (respiratory viruses)
  • Latex agglutination (CSF bacterial antigens).
Techniques
  • ELISA: antigen/antibody capture + enzyme-linked detection antibody → colour change (HIV 4th generation Ag/Ab, hepatitis serology).
  • Agglutination (blood grouping, Widal, ASOT), complement fixation, neutralisation, Western blot (confirmatory), immunofluorescence.
Cell-mediatedIGRA (T-cell IFN-γ release on TB antigens) and Mantoux (type IV skin reaction).
Hepatitis B serologyHBsAg (current infection), anti-HBc IgM (acute), anti-HBc IgG (past exposure), anti-HBs (immunity: vaccinated if anti-HBs only), HBeAg (high infectivity).
Limitations
  • Window period (antibodies take time), immunosuppressed may not mount antibodies, cross-reactivity, maternal antibody in infants (up to 18 months).
  • Molecular tests (PCR) are now often preferred for acute diagnosis.

los.text: Explain the factors that influence parents’ perceptions of risk regarding the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and the determinants that drive their decision whether to vaccinate
los.html:
Background
  • Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper falsely linked MMR to autism
  • Later retracted (2010) and Wakefield struck off for fraud.
  • Large studies show no link.
  • MMR uptake in the UK fell to ~80% (lower in places) → measles outbreaks (e.g. Swansea 2012–13: >1,200 cases, one death).
Factors in parents' risk perception
  • Cognitive biases: omission bias (harm from acting feels worse than harm from not acting), availability heuristic (vivid stories of "vaccine damage"), mistrust of statistics, overestimating vaccine risk and underestimating disease risk (measles now rarely seen: vaccines are victims of their own success).
  • Trust: in government, pharmaceutical industry, healthcare professionals (trust in own GP/HV/nurse is a strong positive influence).
  • Information sources: media, internet, social media misinformation, peers/parent networks.
  • Personal/social: previous experiences, beliefs about "natural" immunity, religious/philosophical beliefs, desire for control and to be a "good parent", social norms in community.
  • Practical: access, convenience, appointment times, missed reminders (often the biggest factor in low uptake in deprived areas, not hesitancy).
ModelsWHO "3 Cs" (Confidence, Complacency, Convenience), later 5 Cs (+ Calculation, Collective responsibility). Health Belief Model.
Improving uptakePresumptive, respectful conversations; address specific concerns; reliable information; reminder/recall; opportunistic vaccination; outreach to under-served groups; tackle misinformation.

los.text: Identify the components of the immune system and link them to function
los.html:
Identify on histology/slides
  • Lymph node: capsule, subcapsular sinus, cortex with follicles (B cells; germinal centres pale), paracortex (T cells, high endothelial venules), medulla (cords with plasma cells, sinuses with macrophages).
  • Spleen: white pulp (periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (T cells) around central arteriole + B-cell follicles), red pulp (cords of Billroth and sinusoids; filters old RBCs).
  • Thymus: lobules with dark cortex (dense thymocytes) and pale medulla with Hassall's corpuscles; involutes with age (fat).
  • Tonsils/MALT/Peyer's patches: lymphoid follicles under epithelium; M cells sample antigen.
  • Bone marrow: haematopoietic cells, megakaryocytes, fat.
Cells on blood filmNeutrophil (multilobed), lymphocyte (round, thin rim), monocyte (large, kidney nucleus), eosinophil (bilobed, orange granules), basophil (dark granules).
Link to function
  • Primary organs → generate and educate lymphocytes
  • Secondary organs → place where antigen meets lymphocytes (lymph nodes sample lymph; spleen samples blood; MALT samples mucosal surfaces)
  • Effector cells mediate killing.

los.text: Identify the component parts of the haemopoietic system and link them to the global structural framework of this system, and relevant interacting systems, with respect to function
los.html:
Haematopoietic stem cell(bone marrow; CD34⁺; self-renewing, multipotent)Common myeloid progenitor (→ erythrocytes, megakaryocytes/platelets, granulocytes, monocytes, mast cells, dendritic cells) and common lymphoid progenitor (→ B cells, T cells, NK cells).
Sites
  • Yolk sac (weeks 3–8) → liver (main fetal site, plus spleen) → bone marrow (from ~5 months fetal).
  • Adults: axial skeleton (pelvis, vertebrae, sternum, ribs, skull) and proximal femur/humerus.
  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis (liver/spleen) in myelofibrosis, thalassaemia.
Marrow structureHaematopoietic cords + sinusoids + stromal "niche" (osteoblasts, endothelium, mesenchymal cells, adipocytes) providing growth factors and adhesion.
Growth factorsEPO (kidney; RBC), TPO (liver; platelets), G-CSF (neutrophils), GM-CSF, IL-3, IL-7 (lymphocytes), SCF.
Interacting systems
  • Lymphoid organs (thymus for T-cell maturation)
  • Spleen (removes old RBCs, stores platelets)
  • Liver (TPO, iron storage, clotting factors)
  • Kidney (EPO)
  • Gut (iron, B12, folate absorption).
ClinicalFBC reflects marrow output; bone marrow aspirate/trephine; failure (aplastic anaemia), infiltration (leukaemia, metastases), stem cell transplant.

los.text: Review the basic structure of immunoglobulins and explain how B cells are able to generate a plethora of antibodies capable of recognising a wide range of antigens
los.html:
• Structure: Y-shaped
    • 2 identical heavy chains + 2 identical light chains (κ or λ) joined by disulfide bonds.
    • Fab (antigen-binding; variable domains V_H + V_L with hypervariable CDRs) and Fc (constant region; determines class and effector functions: complement binding, Fc receptors on phagocytes, placental transfer).
    • Hinge region gives flexibility.
ClassFeatures
IgMPentamer (J chain); first produced; best complement activator; naïve B-cell surface (monomer)
IgGMonomer; most abundant; crosses placenta; opsonisation, neutralisation, complement; memory responses (IgG1–4)
IgADimer in secretions (mucosa, breast milk; secretory component)
IgEBinds mast cells/basophils; allergy, parasites
IgDNaïve B-cell surface receptor
Generating diversity(~10¹¹ specificities)
  • V(D)J recombination (RAG1/2 enzymes): heavy chain joins one V, D and J segment; light chain one V and J (combinatorial diversity).
  • Junctional diversity: imprecise joining, TdT adds nucleotides (N-regions).
  • Heavy–light chain pairing (combinatorial association).
  • Somatic hypermutation (AID) in germinal centres → affinity maturation.
  • Class switch recombination (AID; driven by T-cell cytokines) changes isotype, keeps specificity.
Allelic exclusionEach B cell expresses one specificity.

los.text: Link the structure of the lymphatics and lymphoid organs to their immunological function
los.html:
Lymphatic vessels
  • Blind-ended capillaries take up interstitial fluid, proteins, antigen and dendritic cells
  • → afferent lymphatics
  • → lymph node
  • → efferent lymphatic
  • → thoracic duct
  • → blood.
  • Immune surveillance of every tissue.
Lymph node structure → function
  • Afferent lymph enters subcapsular sinus (macrophages trap antigen)
  • → cortex (B-cell follicles: antigen captured on follicular dendritic cells; germinal centres for affinity maturation)
  • → paracortex (T cells meet dendritic cells; high endothelial venules let naïve lymphocytes enter from blood via L-selectin/CCR7)
  • → medulla (plasma cells secrete antibody into efferent lymph).
  • Swollen nodes during infection = lymphocyte proliferation (reactive lymphadenopathy).
Spleen
  • Filters blood (no afferent lymphatics).
  • Red pulp removes old/abnormal RBCs and encapsulated bacteria
  • White pulp mounts responses to blood-borne antigens
  • Marginal zone B cells respond to polysaccharide (T-independent) antigens → asplenia → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib): vaccines + prophylactic penicillin.
MALT(tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix, BALT)M cells transport luminal antigen to underlying follicles → IgA production; mucosal tolerance.
ThymusEpithelial cells present self-antigen (AIRE) → central tolerance.
Recirculationnaïve lymphocytes circulate blood → nodes → lymph → blood to maximise chance of meeting antigen.

los.text: Describe the process of B cell development and how antibodies are produced as a result of antigen detection
los.html:
Bone marrow development (antigen-independent)
  • HSC
  • → pro-B cell (heavy chain V(D)J rearrangement)
  • → pre-B cell (heavy chain with surrogate light chain = pre-BCR; checkpoint)
  • → immature B cell (light chain rearrangement → surface IgM)
  • → negative selection (self-reactive cells deleted, receptor editing, anergy = central tolerance)
  • → mature naïve B cell (surface IgM + IgD)
  • → leaves marrow to secondary lymphoid organs.
Activation (antigen-dependent)
  • BCR binds antigen → internalised, processed, presented on MHC II.
  • T-cell help: Tfh cell recognises peptide–MHC II → CD40L–CD40 + cytokines (IL-4, IL-21).
  • Germinal centre reaction: proliferation, somatic hypermutation, selection of high-affinity clones on follicular dendritic cells (affinity maturation), class switching (IgG, IgA, IgE).
  • Differentiation into plasma cells (secrete large amounts of antibody; long-lived in bone marrow) and memory B cells.
T-independent responses(polysaccharides)Mainly IgM, little memory.
KineticsPrimary response: lag ~5–7 days, IgM first then IgG. Secondary response: rapid, mostly high-affinity IgG.
Antibody effector functionsNeutralisation, opsonisation, complement activation, ADCC, mast cell sensitisation (IgE).
